title: Reading and Redirecting the Unspoken Step
intro: The chapter above gave the results of the tests for internal reasoning and broadcast. This level gives the designs behind them: what the readouts actually show layer by layer before any intervention, how the two controls are built, and how the broadcast count of 76 of 192 breaks apart when the individual trials are laid out.

chapters.title: Presence first, then cause
chapters.body:
Section 3.3 is built in two halves, and the order matters. The first half establishes only that the unspoken
concept is in the readout at all ([[fig-12]]); the causal claim waits for the second.

The presence half is a depth trace. On the spider prompt, read at its final position, the top [[j-lens-readout]]
token at L67 is *spider*. At L83 the readout splits between *legs*, *eight* and *spider*. At L88 it is *eight*,
and at L99 it is the output digit *8*. Layer numbers here are percentages of depth rather than raw indices
([[layer-percentage-indexing]]), so the handover from the inferred animal to the spoken count occupies the last
third of the network, above the [[workspace-layers]] where the animal appeared.

The poetry panel is read at the line break, before any token of the second line exists. At L54 the alternative
rhyme *light* already sits at rank 3. At L75 the planned rhyme dominates. At L99, one position later, the
readout gives *Prepared*, the word that in fact opens the line ([[rhyme-planning]], scored at scale on the
[[poetry-benchmark]]).

Presence alone would not settle much. The lens is built from the average causal effect of activations on output
tokens, so some agreement between a readout and what the model says is guaranteed by construction
([[report-relation-by-construction]]). That is why the second half applies the [[lens-coordinate-swap]] and
watches the output rather than the readout. The swap is clamped: it is held at every token position for the
whole forward pass ([[activation-clamping]]), so the model cannot quietly recompute the original intermediate at
a later layer and route around the edit ([[fig-13]]).

chapters.title: An intermediate that is neither a fact nor in the answer's language
chapters.body:
Two of the section's four examples do not fit the shape of a bridging fact, and each stretches the claim in a
different direction.

The third example is a prompt written entirely in Chinese, asking for the antonym of 小 ("small"). The model
answers 大 ("big"). At middle layers the readout carries the English tokens *big* and *bigger*, which the paper
reads as the model routing the inference through an English-aligned representation
([[shared-multilingual-representation]]; the systematic version is the 54-prompt [[multilingual-benchmark]]).
Something else sits in the readout beside the antonym. At L50 the top token is *Chinese*: the identity of the
language the answer must come out in is itself a workspace item ([[target-language-representation]]). Swapping
*big* and *bigger* for *long* and *longer* turns the Chinese output into 长 ("long").

The fourth example is not a fact at all. In the [[bandit-choice-prompt]] the model sees a history of A/B choices
ending in A, is told the last outcome made it either happy or sad, and is instructed to consider whether to
repeat or switch before answering with a single character. Both words, *repeat* and *switch*, appear verbatim in
both versions of the prompt.

That is what makes the readout informative. Taking the median over layers L38 to L79, only the strategy the
outcome calls for is strongly present: *repeat* and *continuation* in the happy condition, *switch* and *change*
in the sad one ([[fig-14]]). The [[j-space]] therefore carries the model's selection rather than a copy of the
prompt. Exchanging the two conditions' strategy directions flips the choice in both directions, from A to B and
from B to A.

chapters.title: Two ways the result could have been an artifact
chapters.body:
The depth control turns on a single prediction. If the intermediate's lens vector worked only by carrying some
of the answer's, then swapping the intermediate and swapping the answer would be two names for one intervention,
and both would begin to bite at the same depth. So each swap is applied over different layer ranges, and the
effect is measured as the log-probability difference in the expected output, averaged over successful Sonnet 4.5
trials ([[fig-15]]). The curves separate: the intermediate swap takes effect a median of roughly 17 percent of
depth earlier ([[swap-depth-control]]). The paper reads that as the intermediate being used before the answer
has been computed.

The circularity control needs a representation of the unspoken step that the lens had no hand in building. The
[[intermediate-probe]] is the mean [[residual-stream]] activation over prompts that imply the same intermediate
through different surface cues and ask different questions about it, minus the mean over all intermediates.

That probe is then split. [[gradient-pursuit]] fits a nonnegative combination of $k = 25$ lens vectors to it, and
the leftover is the remainder ([[j-space-component-decomposition]]). The fit is small: it typically accounts for
roughly 10 to 15 percent of the probe's variance.

Four swaps are then scored on 90 two-hop prompts, with [[wilson-interval]] error bars ([[fig-16]]). The raw lens
swap reaches the implied answer on 60 percent of trials and the probe's J-space component on 61 percent, so the
small piece matches the instrument it was built to check. The remainder reaches 28 percent. Under the
[[complement-clamped-swap-control]], with the J-space coordinates held at their clean-pass values, that 28 falls
to 6 — the remainder's effect appears to run through the J-space rather than beside it.
chapters.childScope: Take the two controls apart in full: how [[swap-depth-control]] measures the onset depth of the intermediate swap against the answer swap in [[fig-15]], and how the [[intermediate-probe]] is built without the lens, split by [[gradient-pursuit]] into a [[j-space-component]] and a remainder, and scored across the four swap conditions and the [[complement-clamped-swap-control]] of [[fig-16]].

chapters.title: Depth carries the order of the steps
chapters.body:
The arithmetic example makes depth stand in for time. On "calc: ( 4 + 17 ) * 2 + 7 =" the three required values
are absent from the readout through roughly the first third of the network, climb together, and then separate
near layer 71: 21 reaches rank 1 first, 42 about eight layers later, 49 only in the final layers
([[fig-17]], [[arithmetic-intermediate-ordering]]; the benchmark version is the
[[order-of-operations-benchmark]]).

Reading order off a readout is correlational, so the paper checks it with an intervention. The check is
[[mean-difference-patching]], a corpus-averaged form of [[activation-patching]]: the mean activation over prompts
whose intermediate equals some alternative $v$, minus the mean over prompts where it equals the true value, is
added to the residual stream at one layer $L$. Sweeping $L$ gives a curve of the logit of the answer $v$ implies
minus the logit of 49, and the layer where that curve crosses zero is where the patch flips the prediction.

The crossings land where the lens said they would: around layer 71 for 21, around layer 79 for 42, and only in
the last few layers for 49 ([[fig-88]]). This agreement is what licenses reading a concept's entry depth as the
site of a computation ([[mechanistic-localization]]).

A wiring diagram of the same prompt then marks the limit of the picture ([[fig-89]],
[[j-lens-attribution-graphs]]). The node for 21 arrives already computed, and swapping either operand, 4 or 17,
has essentially no effect, which the paper reads as the first addition happening outside the workspace. The
multiplication arrives fused: a *doubled* node feeds 42, while the literal 2 never appears as a named node and
contributes only through the [[remainder-node]]. Chained steps surface in order, but not every step of the chain
is in the workspace.

chapters.title: One vector, sixteen consumers
chapters.body:
The broadcast test has a counting structure worth stating in full ([[function-template-protocol]]). Four
argument categories — countries, months, animals and number words — carry four function templates each, which is
sixteen templates. Each category supplies four arguments, and each argument can be swapped for the other three,
which is twelve source-target pairs per template. Sixteen templates at twelve pairs each is the 192 trials
([[fig-18]], [[fig-19]]).

The per-trial grids show that the aggregate hides a steep gradient ([[fig-68]]). Each template gets a $4 \times
4$ grid whose diagonal is the unmodified baseline and whose twelve off-diagonal cells are the real trials, so a
category contributes 48. Country swaps land on 42 of those 48. Months succeed partially, animals rarely, and
number relations on none of 48 at standard strength.

Where a swap fails, the top output is usually still the correct answer for the argument written in the prompt,
with the target's answer ranked somewhere below it. Doubling the intervention often brings it up
([[swap-strength-alpha]]), which the paper reads as a swap that moves the activation the right way and not far
enough. The 101 of 192 is therefore a stronger edit rather than a second measurement, and the count at default
strength stays at 76.

[[workspace-loading]] is what the gradient tracks: the [[cosine-similarity]] between the residual stream and a
concept's lens vector, averaged over the argument and readout positions of an unmodified forward pass. Countries
load highest and swap most reliably; number words load lowest. The paper offers two readings of the number-word
failure and decides between neither — the model may compute over small integers outside the workspace, or its
representation of them may simply not align with those tokens' lens vectors, an instance of the
[[single-token-limitation]]. What the test measures is [[global-broadcast]], and [[flexible-generalization]] is
the property it is scored against.
chapters.childScope: Open the broadcast experiment: the [[function-template-protocol]]'s four categories and sixteen templates, the per-trial grids of [[fig-68]] with countries at 42 of 48 and number words at 0 of 48, what doubling to [[swap-strength-alpha]] recovers, and how [[workspace-loading]] in [[fig-19]] predicts which swaps land.
